title: MemOCR: Layout-Aware Visual Memory for Efficient Long-Horizon Reasoning
one_liner: Store long interaction history as a compact visual memory page so important evidence gets more space than low-value detail.
lead: Long-horizon agents accumulate more history than they can carry forward in full. Standard memory systems flatten that history into plain text and spend equal context budget on every word. MemOCR changes that allocation rule. It writes a structured memory page with headings and highlights, renders that page as an image, and lets the agent read from the image later. The point is not visual style for its own sake. The point is variable information density, because some evidence deserves more space while routine detail can be compressed more aggressively.

problem.h2: Why flat text memory wastes scarce context budget
paras: An agent with a long task history cannot keep every detail in active context. A common fix is to summarize the history into text. That still allocates space in a nearly uniform way, so key evidence and low-value filler compete for the same limited budget.

The paper targets this allocation problem directly. If the memory system can devote more area to answer-critical evidence and less area to routine detail, later reasoning can preserve the facts that matter most because the compression policy is based on value rather than on linear text length.

callout.html: Turn memory into a structured visual page with variable emphasis, because a layout can allocate space unevenly across facts and thus preserve high-value evidence under tight budget.

object.object: the form and allocation rule of long-horizon memory

hidden.name: information value per unit of memory space
paras: The key hidden quantity is how much future reasoning value each fact provides relative to the space needed to keep it. Some details matter later because they determine the answer. Others are already resolved and can be compressed heavily.

MemOCR tries to estimate that value through learned layout decisions. The page gives more area and emphasis to evidence that later questions are likely to depend on, because preserving the right few facts is more useful than preserving many low-value facts equally.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark facts that deserve more memory space because later reasoning depends on them.

reads.html: This quantity asks which facts are worth scarce memory space. The method succeeds when it spends more space on answer-critical evidence because that improves later reasoning under tight budget.
The system learns budget-aware memory layouts that allocate variable information density across the preserved history, so later reasoning can recover answer-critical evidence more reliably.

mechanism.h2: Why visual layout can beat flat summaries
paras: Flat text memory compresses mostly by shortening. That is limited because every kept word still occupies roughly the same budget share. A visual page can compress in a richer way by changing area, grouping, emphasis, and ordering. That gives the system more control over which facts remain easy to retrieve later.

The image rendering matters because the downstream model can inspect a page where important evidence is visually prominent. If the memory builder has learned to reserve larger regions for answer-critical facts, later reasoning can recover those facts more reliably because they were not squeezed into the same narrow format as everything else.

Training under several budget levels matters because the best compression policy changes with available space. The system must learn not only how to store memory, but how to degrade gracefully when the budget tightens. Budget-aware training provides that pressure directly.

math.h2: Keep high-value facts under a fixed budget
math.words: A simple summary is to maximize answer quality while fitting the memory page into a fixed budget, because the memory system should spend limited space where it helps later reasoning most.
math.equation: memory_score = answer_quality(memory_page) - alpha * budget_overuse + beta * value_preserved
symbols: later task quality after reading the compressed memory page
penalty on exceeding the allowed memory budget
how far the page exceeds the available space limit
reward on keeping high-value evidence visible
total future-useful information retained in the page

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Page A keeps the task goal and the final clue large, so value_preserved = 8.
Page B keeps many routine notes and shrinks the final clue, so value_preserved = 3.
If both fit the same budget and beta = 2, Page A gains 16 reward from preserved value while Page B gains 6.
Later answers are better with Page A because the answer-critical evidence stayed readable.
The system therefore learns to allocate more space to answer-critical facts.

math.note: The paper's full training setup uses budget-aware reinforcement learning, but the core goal is straightforward: spend limited memory space where it helps later reasoning most because later answer quality depends on preserving the right evidence.

charts.title: MemOCR
charts.note: The paper reports better long-horizon question answering because the memory page preserves more of the evidence that later answers depend on.

items.b: The layout policy can emphasize the wrong facts.
items.html: If the memory builder misjudges future value, it may enlarge unimportant details and shrink answer-critical evidence because the training signal did not identify the true bottleneck.

items.b: Rendered pages can become too dense to read.
items.html: If too many items remain highlighted, the visual memory loses its ranking effect because everything starts competing for space again.

items.b: The value estimate may not transfer across task types.
items.html: A layout policy learned on one family of long-horizon tasks may preserve the wrong details on another family because later evidence needs differ.

The method works when the memory builder learns which facts drive later answers and allocates space accordingly, because then tight context budgets remove low-value detail before they remove answer-critical evidence.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a long-horizon reading task where the system must answer later questions from a long stream of notes and observations. Compare three memory strategies: keep recent text only, write a flat text summary, and build a rendered visual memory page with ranked sections. Evaluate answer quality as the allowed memory budget gets smaller.
The demo should show that the visual page loses quality more slowly under shrinking budget because it allocates memory space by evidence value rather than by uniform text length.
demo.closing: A convincing demo must show stronger retention under severe budget pressure, because the paper's claim is about how memory should be allocated when full history cannot be kept.
